Tibet is the land of the Tibetan Plateau, the highest region on Earth, and the homeland of the Tibetan people. The map shows it from 1000 to 1960: from the centuries after the old Tibetan Empire fell in 842 until China took full control in the 1950s.

For most of that time Tibet was ruled by Buddhist lamas, often under the protection of a stronger neighbour:

  • After 842 the plateau broke into small lordships. Buddhism revived from the 900s, helped by teachers from India such as Atisha, who arrived in 1042. New schools grew around great monasteries.
  • In the 1240s the Mongols reached Tibet. The lamas of Sakya became the Mongols' agents and ruled Tibet under the Yuan emperors.
  • From 1354 the Phagmodrupa family ruled. Tsongkhapa founded the Gelug school, whose head received the title of Dalai Lama from a Mongol khan in 1578.
  • In 1642 Mongol troops made the 5th Dalai Lama ruler of all Tibet, with a government at Lhasa. He began the Potala Palace.
  • From 1720 the Qing emperors kept officials and troops in Lhasa and claimed overlordship, though Tibet largely ran its own affairs.
  • A British invasion reached Lhasa in 1904. After the Qing fell, the 13th Dalai Lama declared Tibet independent in 1913, and it governed itself until 1950.

In 1950 the army of the People's Republic of China invaded, and in 1951 Tibet's leaders signed an agreement accepting Chinese rule. After a failed uprising in 1959, the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India with many followers. In 1965 China made central and western Tibet the Tibet Autonomous Region.
